lessonTitle: DNA Damage and Repair: Base Excision, Nucleotide Excision and Mismatch Repair

blocks.text: A four-year-old child develops blistering sunburn and freckling after only a few minutes outdoors, and by adolescence will probably have skin cancers that are rare under the age of fifty in other people. Her skin cells cannot repair the damage that ultraviolet light does to DNA. How do healthy cells cope, and what happens when the repair machinery fails?

blocks.markdown: Every human cell suffers tens of thousands of DNA lesions per day. Sources of damage include **endogenous** processes (spontaneous deamination of bases, depurination, oxidation by reactive oxygen species, and errors made during replication) and **exogenous** agents (ultraviolet light, ionising radiation, chemicals in tobacco smoke, aflatoxin). Unrepaired damage becomes a permanent **mutation** when the cell next replicates, so cells have several repair pathways. Each pathway is matched to the kind of lesion it handles: small base changes, bulky helix-distorting lesions, or replication mismatches. They share a common logic: *recognise* the damage, *excise* the faulty segment, *resynthesise* using the undamaged complementary strand as a template, and *ligate* the nick.

blocks.title: The three excision repair pathways
blocks.text: Base excision repair (BER) removes a single damaged base. Nucleotide excision repair (NER) removes a short stretch of nucleotides containing a bulky, helix-distorting lesion. Mismatch repair (MMR) removes a stretch of newly synthesised DNA containing a replication error. In all three the undamaged complementary strand is the template for repair.

blocks.markdown: **Base excision repair.** It deals with small, non-bulky lesions such as the **uracil** formed when cytosine is deaminated, or 8-oxoguanine from oxidation. A specific **DNA glycosylase** recognises the abnormal base and cleaves the bond between the base and the sugar, leaving an apurinic/apyrimidinic (AP) site. An **AP endonuclease** cuts the backbone at the site, a DNA polymerase fills the gap with a single nucleotide (short patch), and **DNA ligase** seals the nick. Because the lesion is detected by its chemical identity, BER occurs throughout the cell cycle. Inherited defects in one glycosylase (MUTYH) cause a polyposis condition (MUTYH-associated polyposis).

**Nucleotide excision repair.** Ultraviolet B light links adjacent pyrimidines (usually thymines) on one strand, forming **cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers**. These distort the double helix, so they are recognised by their *shape*, not their chemistry. NER proteins (XPA-XPG, named after the disease xeroderma pigmentosum) unwind the DNA around the lesion, an endonuclease cuts either side to remove an oligonucleotide of about 24-32 nucleotides, and DNA polymerase and ligase fill and seal the gap. NER works in two ways: global genome NER scans the whole genome, and transcription-coupled NER is triggered when RNA polymerase stalls on a lesion in an active gene. NER also removes bulky chemical adducts such as those from tobacco smoke.

blocks.title: Which pathway repairs which lesion?
blocks.prompt: For each lesion, name the repair pathway and the key recognition step: (a) uracil in DNA after cytosine deamination, (b) a thymine-thymine dimer from UV light, (c) a G-T mismatch just after replication.

steps.text: (a) Uracil is a single abnormal base that does not distort the helix. It is recognised chemically by uracil-DNA glycosylase, so the pathway is base excision repair. Cleavage leaves an AP site, which is then cut, filled with one nucleotide and ligated.

(b) A thymine dimer is a bulky lesion that distorts the helix; recognition depends on distortion of the helix. The pathway is nucleotide excision repair, which removes about 24-32 nucleotides around the dimer.

(c) A G-T mispair is a normal base in the wrong position that the polymerase proofreading missed, so it has no chemical abnormality. Mismatch repair recognises the mispair and must work out which strand is the new one (the newly synthesised strand carries the error).

blocks.answer: (a) base excision repair; (b) nucleotide excision repair; (c) mismatch repair.

blocks.markdown: **Mismatch repair.** DNA polymerase makes a wrong base in roughly 1 in $10^5$ nucleotides added; 3'-to-5' proofreading corrects most of these, leaving about 1 error per $10^7$ nucleotides, and mismatch repair improves accuracy by a further factor of about 100 to 1000. MutS-type proteins (MSH2 with MSH6, or MSH2 with MSH3) recognise mismatches and small insertion-deletion loops, and MutL-type proteins (MLH1 with PMS2) recruit the excision machinery. In bacteria, strand discrimination relies on methylation; in humans, it depends on features of the newly synthesised strand such as nicks. The new strand segment is removed and resynthesised. Cells with defective MMR accumulate mutations, especially in **microsatellites** (short repeated sequences such as $(CA)_n$), because replication slippage in repeats goes uncorrected; this is called **microsatellite instability (MSI)**.

rows: Deaminated, oxidised or alkylated single bases
DNA glycosylase (chemical identity of the base)
Replication mismatches and small insertion-deletion loops
MutS homologues (MSH2, MSH6) with MutL homologues (MLH1, PMS2)
Stretch of the newly made strand

blocks.markdown: **Xeroderma pigmentosum (XP).** XP is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by biallelic mutations in NER genes (XPA-XPG). A rarer form, XP variant, affects the translesion polymerase eta. Without NER, thymine dimers formed by sunlight persist, block replication and transcription, and cause mutations in tumour-suppressor genes and oncogenes. Patients have severe sunburn on minimal exposure, early freckling, dry pigmented skin, photophobia and a very high risk of basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma and melanoma at a young age; some also have neurological abnormalities. Management is strict photoprotection. In this recessive condition each parent of an affected child is a heterozygous carrier, and the recurrence risk for each further child is 25%.

**Lynch syndrome (hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer, HNPCC).** Lynch syndrome is an autosomal *dominant* cancer predisposition caused by a heterozygous germline mutation in an MMR gene (most often *MLH1* or *MSH2*, less often *MSH6* or *PMS2*). Everyone in the family with the mutation has one defective copy in every cell, and loss of the second (normal) copy in a colonic cell, as in Knudson's two-hit model, abolishes MMR in that cell. Mutations then accumulate quickly, giving MSI-high tumours. Affected people develop colorectal cancer at a younger age than the general population (often around the mid-40s) with relatively few polyps, and they also have increased risk of endometrial, ovarian, gastric and urothelial cancers. A first-degree relative of a carrier has a 50% chance of carrying the mutation.

blocks.title: Estimating errors left after proofreading and mismatch repair
blocks.prompt: A polymerase has an intrinsic error rate of 1 in $10^5$ nucleotides. Proofreading improves accuracy 100-fold, and mismatch repair a further 100-fold. How many errors would be expected per $2\times10^6$ nucleotides copied after (a) polymerase and proofreading, and (b) after mismatch repair as well?
blocks.answer: (a) 0.2 errors; (b) 0.002 errors per 2 million nucleotides. This shows how each layer of correction multiplies accuracy, and why loss of MMR causes a mutator phenotype.

blocks.title: Link the pathway to the disease
blocks.text: Defective NER leads to xeroderma pigmentosum (autosomal recessive, UV sensitivity, skin cancers). Defective MMR leads to Lynch syndrome (autosomal dominant at the level of the family, early colorectal cancer, MSI). The difference in inheritance reflects that the cancer-prone cells in Lynch syndrome need loss of the second allele, whereas XP needs mutations in both alleles inherited.

items: BER: glycosylase removes one abnormal base, AP endonuclease cuts, one nucleotide is replaced.
NER: bulky helix-distorting lesions (UV dimers) are removed as a 24-32 nucleotide fragment.
MMR: corrects replication mismatches; defects produce microsatellite instability.
XP is autosomal recessive; Lynch syndrome is autosomal dominant.

points: Three excision repair pathways handle different lesions: BER for single abnormal bases, NER for bulky helix-distorting lesions, MMR for replication mismatches.
Defective nucleotide excision repair causes xeroderma pigmentosum: extreme UV sensitivity and early skin cancers.
Defective mismatch repair (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2) causes Lynch syndrome, with microsatellite instability and early colorectal and endometrial cancer.

questions.stem: A cytosine in DNA spontaneously loses its amino group to become uracil. Which repair pathway removes this lesion?

options.text: Base excision repair
Nucleotide excision repair
Mismatch repair
Homologous recombination

distractorRationale.a: Correct: a glycosylase removes uracil, followed by AP endonuclease, polymerase and ligase.
distractorRationale.b: NER removes bulky helix-distorting lesions, not a single abnormal base.
distractorRationale.c: MMR corrects replication errors between normal bases, not an abnormal base like uracil.

questions.explanation: Uracil is a small, chemically abnormal base recognised by uracil-DNA glycosylase, which starts base excision repair. The helix is not significantly distorted, so NER is not required.

questions.stem: Which feature best distinguishes nucleotide excision repair from base excision repair?

options.text: NER removes an oligonucleotide containing a helix-distorting lesion, whereas BER removes a single base via a glycosylase
NER occurs only in bacteria, whereas BER occurs only in humans
NER uses the damaged strand as the template, whereas BER uses the undamaged strand
NER requires DNA ligase, whereas BER does not

questions.correctOptionText: NER removes an oligonucleotide containing a helix-distorting lesion, whereas BER removes a single base via a glycosylase

distractorRationale.a: Correct: that is the defining difference in lesion and excision size.
distractorRationale.b: Both pathways exist in humans and bacteria.
distractorRationale.c: Both pathways use the undamaged strand as a template.
distractorRationale.d: Both pathways require DNA ligase to seal the nick.

questions.explanation: NER recognises distortion of the helix and cuts out a stretch of roughly 24-32 nucleotides, while BER recognises a single abnormal base with a glycosylase and replaces one nucleotide. Both use the intact complementary strand as the template and both use a ligase.

questions.stem: A boy of 6 has developed multiple freckles on sun-exposed skin and several basal cell carcinomas. His parents are healthy and unrelated carriers of the same condition. What is the underlying defect?

options.text: Inability to excise UV-induced pyrimidine dimers by nucleotide excision repair
Inability to correct replication mismatches
Inability to remove deaminated cytosine
Loss of DNA ligase activity in all tissues

questions.correctOptionText: Inability to excise UV-induced pyrimidine dimers by nucleotide excision repair

distractorRationale.b: Defective MMR causes Lynch syndrome, with colorectal and endometrial cancer, not early UV-driven skin cancers.
distractorRationale.c: Defects in BER glycosylases lead to polyposis rather than the UV phenotype.
distractorRationale.d: Complete ligase loss would not be compatible with this picture; it is not the cause of XP.

questions.explanation: Severe photosensitivity with skin cancers in childhood and recessive inheritance (healthy carrier parents) indicate xeroderma pigmentosum. Pyrimidine dimers from UV light are not removed by NER, so they accumulate and cause mutations.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old woman has endometrial cancer. Her father had colon cancer at 44 and her paternal aunt had colon cancer at 49. Tumour testing shows microsatellite instability. Which gene defect is the most likely cause?

options.text: Germline mutation in a mismatch repair gene such as MSH2
Germline mutation in a nucleotide excision repair gene such as XPA
Somatic mutation in a base excision glycosylase only
Mutation in a DNA ligase gene

questions.correctOptionText: Germline mutation in a mismatch repair gene such as MSH2

distractorRationale.a: Correct: early cancers in several relatives with MSI suggest Lynch syndrome.
distractorRationale.b: XPA mutations cause xeroderma pigmentosum, a recessive UV disorder.
distractorRationale.c: A purely somatic glycosylase mutation would not explain a family pattern or MSI.
distractorRationale.d: Ligase defects are not the cause of the Lynch pattern.

questions.explanation: Early-onset colorectal and endometrial cancers in related individuals together with microsatellite instability indicate Lynch syndrome, from a germline mutation in an MMR gene. MSI results because replication slippage errors in repeat sequences go uncorrected.

questions.stem: Why does Lynch syndrome behave as an autosomal dominant condition in families even though mismatch repair is lost only when both gene copies are inactive in a cell?

options.text: Carriers inherit one defective allele in every cell, so only one further somatic hit is needed to abolish MMR in a given cell
The mutant protein inactivates the normal protein by dominant-negative interference in every cell
Mismatch repair genes are located on the X chromosome
Carriers have too much mismatch repair protein

questions.correctOptionText: Carriers inherit one defective allele in every cell, so only one further somatic hit is needed to abolish MMR in a given cell

distractorRationale.a: Correct: this is the two-hit model; the germline hit is already present.
distractorRationale.b: A dominant-negative mechanism is not the usual explanation for Lynch syndrome; the cancer risk comes from loss of the second allele.
distractorRationale.c: MMR genes such as MLH1 and MSH2 are autosomal.
distractorRationale.d: The mechanism is loss of function, not excess protein.

questions.explanation: Everyone who inherits a mutation has one functioning copy, which is enough for normal repair until a somatic mutation, deletion or silencing removes the second copy in a colonic or endometrial cell. Because the first hit is already present in every cell, cancer risk is high and the family pattern is dominant.

questions.stem: After proofreading, a human DNA polymerase leaves about 1 uncorrected error per 10,000,000 nucleotides copied. Mismatch repair corrects 99% of these. How many uncorrected errors are expected when a diploid genome of 6,000,000,000 nucleotides is copied in a cell with fully functional mismatch repair? Give your answer as a number of errors.
questions.explanation: Errors after proofreading equal 6,000,000,000 divided by 10,000,000, which is 600. Mismatch repair removes 99%, leaving 1% of 600 = 6. Without functional MMR (as in Lynch syndrome tumour cells) the full 600 would persist.

questions.stem: True or false: A person with xeroderma pigmentosum can repair UV-induced pyrimidine dimers normally but cannot repair mismatches introduced during replication.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Xeroderma pigmentosum is a defect in nucleotide excision repair, so UV-induced pyrimidine dimers are not removed. Mismatch repair is generally intact, and defects of that pathway cause Lynch syndrome instead.

questions.stem: Compare base excision repair, nucleotide excision repair and mismatch repair in terms of the lesion each repairs, how the lesion is recognised and the size of the segment removed.
markingGuide: BER repairs single damaged bases (deamination, oxidation, alkylation); recognised by a specific DNA glycosylase; one nucleotide replaced after AP endonuclease cleavage.
NER repairs bulky helix-distorting lesions such as UV pyrimidine dimers; recognised through distortion of the helix; oligonucleotide of about 24-32 nucleotides removed.
MMR repairs replication mismatches and small insertion-deletion loops; recognised by MutS homologues (MSH2/MSH6) with MutL homologues (MLH1/PMS2); a stretch of newly made strand removed.
All use the undamaged strand as a template, then polymerase and ligase.
questions.explanation: Each pathway is matched to a lesion type and recognition mechanism. They share the same strategy of excision, resynthesis against the intact strand and ligation.

questions.stem: A child with xeroderma pigmentosum has developed multiple skin cancers by age 10. Explain the molecular basis of the condition, its inheritance, and why skin cancer develops so early.
markingGuide: UV light forms cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers between adjacent pyrimidines (e.g. thymines).
Nucleotide excision repair (XP genes XPA-XPG) normally removes a 24-32 nucleotide segment containing the dimer.
Mutations in both alleles of an NER gene prevent excision, so dimers persist.
Unrepaired dimers block replication and cause mutations in oncogenes and tumour suppressor genes in sun-exposed skin, leading to early BCC, SCC and melanoma.
Autosomal recessive: parents are carriers; recurrence risk 25%.
questions.explanation: Sun-exposed skin cells accumulate unrepaired UV lesions because NER fails. Mutations in cancer genes accumulate very early, so tumours appear in childhood.

questions.stem: Explain how impaired mismatch repair leads to hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer (Lynch syndrome). Include the role of the two-hit model and of microsatellite instability.
markingGuide: Germline heterozygous mutation in MMR gene (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6 or PMS2); autosomal dominant inheritance with 50% transmission risk.
Second allele lost somatically in a colonic cell (two-hit model), abolishing MMR in that cell.
Replication errors, particularly slippage in microsatellite repeats, are not corrected, causing microsatellite instability.
Mutations accumulate in cancer-relevant genes with repeats, leading to early colorectal cancer, often with few polyps; also endometrial and other cancers.
questions.explanation: The inherited first hit leaves one working allele; loss of the second causes a mutator phenotype. Uncorrected slippage in microsatellites produces MSI and rapid accumulation of oncogenic mutations.
